nameStory: Summer cypress gets its name from its feathery, cypress-like foliage that creates a neat, rounded shrub shape during the growing season. Despite looking like a miniature evergreen, it's actually an annual herb that dies back each winter, hence the 'summer' part of its name.
description: Summer cypress is a bushy annual plant that grows into a neat, oval-shaped mound resembling a small evergreen shrub. It typically reaches 2-4 feet tall and wide, with dense, fine-textured foliage that starts out bright green in summer. The plant is famous for its dramatic fall color change, when the entire plant turns brilliant red or orange, earning it nicknames like 'burningbush' and 'Mexican firebrush.' Originally from Eurasia, it has spread throughout North America and is occasionally found in New England.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a perfectly rounded, dense bush that looks remarkably like a small evergreen shrub, but is actually a soft-stemmed annual herb that you can easily bend or break

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, linear leaves about 1-3 inches long that feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, densely packed on branches in an alternate pattern, giving the plant its feathery cypress-like appearance

idTips.label: Fall Color
idTips.description: Entire plant transforms into brilliant red, orange, or pink in autumn, creating a stunning fiery globe that's visible from far away

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish flowers tucked into leaf joints that you might miss entirely - they lack petals and don't look like typical flowers

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, papery winged seeds develop in late summer and fall, helping the plant spread on the wind

habitat: Summer cypress thrives in disturbed, well-drained soils and is most commonly found along roadsides, in vacant lots, agricultural edges, and waste places. In New England, look for it in sunny, open areas with sandy or gravelly soil, particularly near human activity. It prefers areas that have been recently disturbed and doesn't compete well in established plant communities.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up, producing small green seedlings that quickly develop their characteristic bushy shape.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly into dense, bright green mounds and produce their tiny flowers. The cypress-like foliage is at its most lush and convincing evergreen appearance.
seasonality.fall: The spectacular color change occurs, turning brilliant red, orange, or pink. Seeds mature and disperse on the wind during this time.
seasonality.winter: Plants are completely dead and may persist as brown, dried skeletons, or break apart and blow away, leaving only seeds to start the cycle again.

funFact: Summer cypress was actually grown as an ornamental 'World's Fair plant' in American gardens during the early 1900s because of its perfect symmetrical shape and stunning fall color - but it liked our climate so much that it escaped cultivation and now grows wild across the continent!
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for young evergreen trees or shrubs, especially small arborvitae or juniper, but remember that summer cypress is soft to the touch and herbaceous - if you can easily bend or break a branch, it's not a real evergreen! Real evergreens have woody stems and needle-like leaves that stay green year-round.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this 'burningbush' with the common landscape shrub burning bush (Euonymus alatus) - summer cypress is an annual herb while the landscape burning bush is a woody perennial shrub. The similar common names come from their shared tendency to turn brilliant red in fall.
compareHints: Summer cypress is the only member of the Bassia genus commonly found in New England. Within the amaranth family, it's most similar to lamb's quarters (Chenopodium album), but lamb's quarters has broader, diamond-shaped leaves and grows as a more open, weedy plant rather than the dense, shrub-like form of summer cypress. Summer cypress is unique in its family for mimicking the appearance of an evergreen shrub.
